newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.N. says Asia has world's worst refugee problems.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Asia has world's worst refugee problems.

text.p: Ethnic strife and political upheaval in Asia has contributed to a major rise in the number of refugees in the world, the head of the United Nations refugee agency said on Wednesday.

"The UNHCR's work has expanded considerably...in 1991 it was responsible for 17 million people in the world. In 1996 the figure rose to 26.1 million people," said Ogata, the United Nations High Comissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

Ogata told officials from 13 countries attending a U.N. conference held in Amman on mass population displacement in Asia that world figures include 13.2 million refugees forced to flee abroad, and 3.3 million former refugees who returned home but needed UNHCR's reintegration into their communities.
Some 4.7 million displaced people fled inside their own countries and some 4.9 million were in refugee-like situations, such as war victims in former Yugoslavia.

Ogata said the UNHCR's annual budget rose to $1.2 billion. She said the scale of the refugee problems in Central Asia, Southwest Asia and the Middle East was greater than in any other region in the world.
The UNHCR spent $1.4 billion since 1979 just in South West Asia, assisting in the return and reintegration of more than five million Afghans, Iraqis and Tajiks during the last six years alone.

"This record is unparalleled in any part of the world," Ogata said, adding that "the UNCHR was working to increase its presence in countries of origin of refugees to deploy assistance and protection on both sides of the border".
Displacement in Central and Southwest Asia was worsened in recent years by the dissolution of the former Soviet Union and a marked upsurge of conflict within states, Ogata said.

Citing Afghanistan which has since 1979 seen the greatest displacement problem ever in the region, Ogata said although three million Afghanis have been repatriated since from an original six million people, the problem persisted.

UNHCR channelled over $30 million since 1993 in Central Asia, including operations in Tajikistan with over two-thirds of the internally displaced refugees now rehabilitated after a civil war which affected some 600,000 people.

Ogata, saying operations in Pakistan alone cost $1.02 billion, expressed concern about declining donor willingness to finance long-term refugee operations. Many donors were constrained by "a combination of dwindling resources on the one hand and profilerating humanitarian crisis on the other".
Burden-sharing was needed to help countries of asylum in coping with refugee problems and countries of origin in reintegrating refugees and resuming growth, Ogata said.
